query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Short-time, high-temperature spark plasma infiltration of a W preform or ligament with Cu (at approximately 1100–1200°C under moderate pressure) can rapidly densify the interface to prevent phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby leading to improved thermal conductivity under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to plasma‐facing joints.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite with tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments dispersed within a copper matrix.
generation.intervention: Apply spark plasma infiltration with a brief dwell time at ~1100–1200°C under moderate pressure to achieve rapid and full densification of the W–Cu interface.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled high-temperature (1100–1200°C) and short sintering times with moderate pressure; service conditions include high heat flux and irradiation typical of plasma-facing joints between W-based materials and Cu-based cooling systems.
generation.structural_mediator: A highly densified, well-bonded interface between tungsten and copper that minimizes interfacial porosity and suppresses phase separation.
generation.mechanism: The rapid, high-temperature infiltration process minimizes the time available for detrimental interdiffusion and coarsening, thus stabilizing the interfacial microstructure and preventing void nucleation. As a result, the optimized interface enhances thermal conduction across the composite under severe operating conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated composite will exhibit a significantly higher thermal conductivity and a more stable interfacial microstructure compared to an untreated composite, which suffers from phase separation and void formation under service conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites processed by conventional methods that require longer dwell times and tend to develop phase separation and interfacial voids when subjected to high heat-flux and irradiation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable within processing windows that permit rapid densification without provoking excessive interdiffusion, and for joints operating within the typical thermal and irradiation environments of plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimization of temperature, pressure, and dwell time to fully prevent interfacial defects without inducing unwanted interdiffusion requires further investigation. Scale-up effects and reproducibility under industrial conditions remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one using conventional sintering (control) and the other using the proposed short-time, high-temperature spark plasma infiltration. Subject both sets to simulated plasma-facing joint conditions, including high heat flux and irradiation. Post-treatment, perform a detailed microstructural analysis and thermal conductivity measurement.
measurements: Thermal conductivity tests under controlled thermal gradients
Scanning/transmission electron microscopy to assess interfacial voids and phase separation
X-ray diffraction to detect any abnormal phase formation
Irradiation exposure tests to evaluate interface stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the spark plasma infiltrated composite does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity and fails to show reduced interfacial void formation and phase separation compared to the control sample under identical service conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Powder metallurgy is a solid-state process that usually includes mechanical alloying (MA) or milling, followed by shaping and a sintering cycle for the consolidation of the powder. Previous work on AlCrCuFeMnNi CCA obtained by pressureless sintering (PLS) showed that the formation of a liquid phase during sintering favours the coalescence and heterogeneous distribution of oxide particles, which decreases the hardness of the obtained samples []. However, the absence of a liquid phase during this thermal cycle by decreasing the temperature can cause poor densification, limiting the properties of CCA processed by PLS. Samples with high densification can be obtained by sintering without the presence of a liquid phase through techniques such as spark plasma or hot pressing sintering. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) is one of the most common techniques reported in the literature for sintering CCAs obtained by MA [,]. Despite the very fast sintering cycles and heating rates, this technique requires highly specialised equipment [,]. Hot pressing sintering (HPS) uses relatively simple equipment compared to SPS and can produce samples with high relative densities and good mechanical properties.

Nuclear fusion-based power reactors require advancements with regard to high-temperature and plasma-facing materials in order to prevent degradation due to the exposure to high-temperature and high-energy neutron flux produced during deuterium-tritium fusion reactions. The severity of the service environment is expected to increase in upcoming fusion reactors with increased power ratings and those under transient scenarios. For instance, the heat load on the divertor, a key component of the tokamak design, , is expected to increase to 10 MW/m2 (steady state) and 20 MW/m2 (transient for 10 seconds). The inner and outer vertical targets of the divertor, where the kinetic energy of plasma particles is converted into heat, must withstand loads up to ~7–40 MJ/m2 and ~4–25 MJ/m2, respectively, under plasma disruption, . Therefore, unprecedented thermal, mechanical and physical characteristics are required for fusion reactor materials.

decision.trend: None of the listed earlier works addresses tungsten–copper composites or the specific challenge of mitigating phase separation and interfacial void formation under heat-transfer and irradiation. The surveyed papers focus on different matrix/reinforcement systems (e.g., high-entropy alloys with diamond, magnesium, steel, diboride ceramics, or carbide particles) and do not examine W–Cu under plasma-facing joint conditions. Thus, the long-standing challenge of stabilizing W–Cu interfaces in harsh environments remains unaddressed by these studies.
decision.unsolved: How to reliably prevent phase separation and interfacial void formation in W–Cu composites under the severe thermal and irradiation environment relevant to plasma-facing joints—while maintaining high thermal conductivity—remains an open question, with no direct solutions provided in the surveyed literature.
decision.lever: Employ short-time, high-temperature spark plasma infiltration of W preforms or ligaments with Cu (∼1100–1200 °C for minimal dwell time, under moderate pressure) to achieve rapid, full densification and a stable interface before detrimental interdiffusion or voids can develop during service.
decision.why: A tightly controlled, fast consolidation route can minimize microstructural coarsening and porosity at the W–Cu interface, reducing phase separation rates and void nucleation. Prompt compaction under localized high heating rates aids in preserving a stable interface and enhances final thermal conductivity under the high loads and irradiation conditions of plasma-facing applications.
